bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Returns disclosed for FY26: ROE 20.12% and ROCE 29.10% (FY23: 27.45% / 37.89%; FY24: 14.40% / 21.49%; FY25: 17.15% / 25.81%); the snapshot slide rounds these to "ROCE: 29%" and "ROE: 20%".
- Net worth grew 925 → 2,075 → 2,450 → 2,998 INR Mn across FY23-FY26, with growth funded from retained earnings — Equity Share Capital unchanged at INR 400 Mn through FY24-FY26.
- Net D/E charted at 0.95x (FY23), 0.26x (FY24), 0.34x (FY25) and 0.46x (FY26); FY26 borrowings were INR 1,184 Mn current and INR 225 Mn non-current.
- Working capital is inventory-heavy: inventories INR 3,357 Mn in FY26 (FY25: 2,923; FY24: 2,242) against total assets of INR 4,860 Mn; trade receivables jumped to INR 558 Mn in FY26 from INR 173 Mn in FY25.
- Shareholding as on 30th June 2026: Promoters 75.00%, AIF 0.01%, Public 24.99%. The deck makes no mention of dividends or buybacks.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- End-to-end manufacturing strength — one of India's most established organised jewellery manufacturing set-ups, blending artisanal handcraft with precision machine-based production
- Diversified client base via a dual-channel model — institutional B2B clients across regional and national retail networks alongside its own B2C brand, Harit Zaveri
- In-house design and quality assurance capability, particularly in the lightweight and antique jewellery categories
- Established leadership in the Jadau, Meena and Kundan antique gold niche built over three decades
- Pan India wholesale distribution network reaching national, regional and local jewellers
- Legacy and deep-rooted promoter involvement supporting trust with institutional partners and retail customers
- Post-listing momentum since listing in FY24 — strengthened governance, reporting discipline and market visibility
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Competition risk in new geographies (rated LOW) — As RBZ plans to expand into Surat, Rajkot, Maninagar (East Ahmedabad) and Gandhinagar, it faces established local and national jewellers with strong regional brand recall, potentially slowing store ramp-up and customer acquisition. Mitigation cited: manufacturing strength, design innovation and quality certification, brand visibility through audio-visual films, B2C exhibitions and digital campaigns, and a phased city-by-city rollout to build local trust before scaling.
- Financial risk from debt-funded expansion and inventory build (rated MODERATE) — Expansion plans rely significantly on debt and internal accruals, with an estimated inventory requirement of around Rs 350 crore for new stores, expected to raise the debt-to-equity ratio and increase sensitivity to interest costs and cash flow management. Mitigation cited: established bank sanctions, a ratings upgrade with positive outlook on credit facilities, and Gold Metal Loan limits held under control as a hedging tool.
- Pricing pressure on making charges and margins (rated MODERATE) — Intense competition from both organised and unorganised players plus rising consumer price sensitivity could compel RBZ to compete more aggressively on making charges and margins, particularly in mass-market and job-work segments. Mitigation cited: value differentiation through design uniqueness, hallmark certification, lightweight/antique offerings and 'Right Price-Fair Price' retail practices rather than price alone.
- Regulatory risk from gold import duty and hallmarking/taxation norms — Recent increases in gold import duty and evolving hallmarking or taxation norms have created near-term uncertainty, with management itself flagging these developments as unfavourable and prompting a deferral of formal FY27 guidance. Mitigation cited: close engagement with industry bodies and monitoring of regulatory developments to adapt sourcing and pricing strategies promptly.
- Gold price volatility and hedging risk — Continued volatility in gold prices, driven in part by global geopolitical developments, challenges RBZ's hedging strategies and cost management with a direct bearing on margins. To mitigate inventory price risk the Company maintains ready infrastructure for Gold Metal Loan (GML) and derivative positions through MCX/NCDX.
- Rising competitive intensity in wedding and bridal jewellery — New entrants targeting the wedding and bridal jewellery segment could increase competitive pressure in one of RBZ's more important revenue categories, potentially affecting pricing power and market share over time.
- Talent retention in a tightening craftsman and retail labour market — Retaining skilled talent remains important to RBZ, particularly as competition for experienced craftsmen and retail personnel intensifies across the industry — a direct constraint on a business whose output depends on artisanal skill and on staffing a rapidly expanding store network.
- Inventory integrity and control risk across a growing store network — The Company relies on unique barcoding of every jewellery piece integrated with its ERP system, daily showroom reconciliations, periodic weight verification by regional teams and prudent gold hedging to maintain inventory accuracy and accountability — controls whose importance scales with the retail rollout. SAP (S/4HANA) was implemented during the year to strengthen internal controls.

outlook.title: Guidance

outlook.body: Expansion into 4 stores in Gujarat (Surat, Rajkot, Gandhinagar, Maninagar); potential future entry into other states post-Gujarat dominance; digital campaigns driving daily wear and occasion wear demand
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Three stated priorities: trust as the enduring competitive advantage, broadening consumer reach, and scaling the consumer franchise
- Transition from a manufacturing-led business to a consumer-focused retail franchise, while manufacturing and wholesale continue to provide the foundation
- Build a leading organised jewellery retail chain in Gujarat, where organised chain penetration is considerably lower than in many other large states
- Expand the retail footprint with planned store additions across Surat, Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Ahmedabad, including large-format stores in Surat and Rajkot during FY27 and a mix of large- and mid-format stores in Eastern Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar
- Expand beyond bridal into contemporary, lightweight and everyday-wear collections, with pilot programmes in daily wear and encouraging traction in 18-carat offerings
- Leverage design-led, vertically integrated manufacturing — in-house designers from leading design institutes, skilled artisans and advanced technology — to sustain differentiation in antique bridal jewellery
- Invest in brand building and digital engagement, targeted digital initiatives, customer engagement programmes and participation in leading exhibitions to deepen consumer connect
- Maintain a transparent transaction framework in which every customer purchase is completed only through formal banking channels, with no acceptance of cash payments
- Optimise inventory and expand relevant product offerings in response to lightweight, exchange-led and value-conscious buying
- Pursue a measured, research-driven approach to entering adjacent categories rather than opening stores for their own sake, aiming at a scalable, sustainable and profitable retail ecosystem
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: RBZ's expansion is framed as "Vision 2027", a plan built around deepening presence in Gujarat by strengthening the retail footprint and extending into new geographies while deepening connect with existing markets. On the retail side the Company is targeting 4 new showrooms across Gujarat over the next two financial years, of which two are scheduled to launch by Q2-FY27. The SWOT restates the same rollout as four new stores in FY27, with Surat and Rajkot as flagship (large size) showrooms of approximately 10,000 sq.ft and Maninagar (East Ahmedabad) and Gandhinagar in the mid-size category at around 5,000 sq.ft each. For Rajkot the disclosure names a prominent location, 10,000 sq.ft area, leased ownership and an 18-year lease tenure; the expected-launch line is cut off mid-word in this bundle. On the manufacturing side the Company is targeting maximum utilisation of existing manufacturing capacity by FY26 and states it is prepared to expand current capacity based on future demand requirements. The existing base is a fully-owned, state-of-the-art facility on the Sarkhej-Gandhinagar Highway in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, spanning approximately 23,966 square feet, designed to accommodate up to 200 skilled artisans and 200 employees, with an annual production capacity of over 2 tons and cutting-edge advanced casting, laser and 3D printing equipment supporting an end-to-end in-house manufacturing setup with select outsourcing. The wholesale footprint it feeds spans over 190 retailers across more than 72 cities in 20 states. Management has also flagged that a ratings upgrade with a positive outlook on its credit facilities strengthens its ability to raise further capital on favourable terms to support these expansion plans, while noting that competitive intensity in the new markets could slow store maturity and payback and add execution risk.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Record gold prices have changed the composition of demand rather than simply reducing it — India's gold jewellery volumes fell 19% year-on-year to 66 tonnes in Q1 2026 while value demand rose 47% year-on-year to a record Rs 999 billion
- Shift towards lightweight jewellery with lower making charges and rising demand for lower-purity 18k and 14k pieces amid heightened price sensitivity
- Exchange-for-old-gold transactions have become a significant share of retail activity as customers manage rising costs
- Divergence between segments — high-income customers continue to buy heavier pieces regardless of price, while mass-market buyers reduce purchases or shift to lower-carat, lighter or studded items
- Wedding and needs-based purchases remain a stable source of underlying demand, providing a floor even as discretionary buying softens
- Organised segment expected to gain market share from approximately 36-38% in FY24 to about 42-43% by FY28, reflecting increasing preference for trusted and compliant brands (Deloitte)
- Indian gems and jewellery market estimated to reach approximately USD 130 billion by 2030; the domestic market was valued at approximately USD 85 billion in early 2026
- Increasing formalisation, mandatory BIS hallmarking, GST compliance and digital manufacturing technologies driving structural transformation of the sector
- Resilient Indian macro backdrop — FY25 real GDP growth of 6.5% with FY26 forecasts between 6.9% and 7%, driven largely by domestic consumption
- Government's recent decision to raise the effective import duty on gold expected to weigh further on demand; ratings agencies have flagged that organised gold jewellery sales volumes could see one of their weakest years in a decade
- US tariffs on Indian goods, which had reached as high as 50% in 2025, were reduced to an effective 18% following a bilateral trade deal announced in February 2026; for a domestic-facing jeweller the effect is indirect, via gold price volatility, import costs and consumer sentiment
- Trade agreements — the India-UK CETA alongside the existing India-UAE CEPA — expected to provide duty advantages and unlock long-term export opportunities for Indian jewellery manufacturers
- Rupee depreciation from roughly Rs 35 to Rs 87-88 against the US dollar over three decades acts as a persistent tailwind under Indian gold prices
- Success of the Ahmedabad flagship store reinforcing management's belief in the opportunity to build an organised retail jewellery network across Gujarat
- Antique bridal jewellery continues to enjoy strong customer acceptance owing to craftsmanship, design differentiation and emotional appeal during wedding purchases
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Revenue and profitability grew strongly on festive demand and retail expansion, with EBITDA margin expanding 63bps QoQ and PAT up 36% YoY; the shift toward higher-margin retail and job work, coupled with strategic store expansion in Gujarat, is redefining the growth trajectory beyond wholesale dependency.

currentContext.expansion: RBZ's expansion is framed as "Vision 2027", a plan built around deepening presence in Gujarat by strengthening the retail footprint and extending into new geographies while deepening connect with existing markets. On the retail side the Company is targeting 4 new showrooms across Gujarat over the next two financial years, of which two are scheduled to launch by Q2-FY27. The SWOT restates the same rollout as four new stores in FY27, with Surat and Rajkot as flagship (large size) showrooms of approximately 10,000 sq.ft and Maninagar (East Ahmedabad) and Gandhinagar in the mid-size category at around 5,000 sq.ft each. For Rajkot the disclosure names a prominent location, 10,000 sq.ft area, leased ownership and an 18-year lease tenure; the expected-launch line is cut off mid-word in this bundle. On the manufacturing side the Company is targeting maximum utilisation of existing manufacturing capacity by FY26 and states it is prepared to expand current capacity based on future demand requirements. The existing base is a fully-owned, state-of-the-art facility on the Sarkhej-Gandhinagar Highway in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, spanning approximately 23,966 square feet, designed to accommodate up to 200 skilled artisans and 200 employees, with an annual production capacity of over 2 tons and cutting-edge advanced casting, laser and 3D printing equipment supporting an end-to-end in-house manufacturing setup with select outsourcing. The wholesale footprint it feeds spans over 190 retailers across more than 72 cities in 20 states. Management has also flagged that a ratings upgrade with a positive outlook on its credit facilities strengthens its ability to raise further capital on favourable terms to support these expansion plans, while noting that competitive intensity in the new markets could slow store maturity and payback and add execution risk.

risks.risk: Competition risk in new geographies (rated LOW)
risks.note: As RBZ plans to expand into Surat, Rajkot, Maninagar (East Ahmedabad) and Gandhinagar, it faces established local and national jewellers with strong regional brand recall, potentially slowing store ramp-up and customer acquisition. Mitigation cited: manufacturing strength, design innovation and quality certification, brand visibility through audio-visual films, B2C exhibitions and digital campaigns, and a phased city-by-city rollout to build local trust before scaling.

risks.risk: Financial risk from debt-funded expansion and inventory build (rated MODERATE)
risks.note: Expansion plans rely significantly on debt and internal accruals, with an estimated inventory requirement of around Rs 350 crore for new stores, expected to raise the debt-to-equity ratio and increase sensitivity to interest costs and cash flow management. Mitigation cited: established bank sanctions, a ratings upgrade with positive outlook on credit facilities, and Gold Metal Loan limits held under control as a hedging tool.

risks.risk: Pricing pressure on making charges and margins (rated MODERATE)
risks.note: Intense competition from both organised and unorganised players plus rising consumer price sensitivity could compel RBZ to compete more aggressively on making charges and margins, particularly in mass-market and job-work segments. Mitigation cited: value differentiation through design uniqueness, hallmark certification, lightweight/antique offerings and 'Right Price-Fair Price' retail practices rather than price alone.

risks.risk: Regulatory risk from gold import duty and hallmarking/taxation norms
risks.note: Recent increases in gold import duty and evolving hallmarking or taxation norms have created near-term uncertainty, with management itself flagging these developments as unfavourable and prompting a deferral of formal FY27 guidance. Mitigation cited: close engagement with industry bodies and monitoring of regulatory developments to adapt sourcing and pricing strategies promptly.

risks.risk: Gold price volatility and hedging risk
risks.note: Continued volatility in gold prices, driven in part by global geopolitical developments, challenges RBZ's hedging strategies and cost management with a direct bearing on margins. To mitigate inventory price risk the Company maintains ready infrastructure for Gold Metal Loan (GML) and derivative positions through MCX/NCDX.

risks.risk: Rising competitive intensity in wedding and bridal jewellery
risks.note: New entrants targeting the wedding and bridal jewellery segment could increase competitive pressure in one of RBZ's more important revenue categories, potentially affecting pricing power and market share over time.

risks.risk: Talent retention in a tightening craftsman and retail labour market
risks.note: Retaining skilled talent remains important to RBZ, particularly as competition for experienced craftsmen and retail personnel intensifies across the industry — a direct constraint on a business whose output depends on artisanal skill and on staffing a rapidly expanding store network.

risks.risk: Inventory integrity and control risk across a growing store network
risks.note: The Company relies on unique barcoding of every jewellery piece integrated with its ERP system, daily showroom reconciliations, periodic weight verification by regional teams and prudent gold hedging to maintain inventory accuracy and accountability — controls whose importance scales with the retail rollout. SAP (S/4HANA) was implemented during the year to strengthen internal controls.

one-line thesis: Revenue and profitability grew strongly on festive demand and retail expansion, with EBITDA margin expanding 63bps QoQ and PAT up 36% YoY; the shift toward higher-margin retail and job work, coupled with strategic store expansion in Gujarat, is redefining the growth trajectory beyond wholesale dependency.

business_model.body: RBZ Jewellers manufactures gold jewellery with a specialisation in intricately crafted Jadau, Meena and Kundan antique bridal and occasion pieces, from an integrated, technologically advanced facility in Ahmedabad. The business spans wholesale supply to leading national retailers, regional jewellers and local family-owned stores across 19 states and 72 cities, alongside contract manufacturing and job work for national jewellery brands. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Record gold prices have changed the composition of demand rather than simply reducing it — India's gold jewellery volumes fell 19% year-on-year to 66 tonnes in Q1 2026 while value demand rose 47% year-on-year to a record Rs 999 billion
- Shift towards lightweight jewellery with lower making charges and rising demand for lower-purity 18k and 14k pieces amid heightened price sensitivity
- Exchange-for-old-gold transactions have become a significant share of retail activity as customers manage rising costs
- Divergence between segments — high-income customers continue to buy heavier pieces regardless of price, while mass-market buyers reduce purchases or shift to lower-carat, lighter or studded items
- Wedding and needs-based purchases remain a stable source of underlying demand, providing a floor even as discretionary buying softens
- Organised segment expected to gain market share from approximately 36-38% in FY24 to about 42-43% by FY28, reflecting increasing preference for trusted and compliant brands (Deloitte)
- Indian gems and jewellery market estimated to reach approximately USD 130 billion by 2030; the domestic market was valued at approximately USD 85 billion in early 2026
- Increasing formalisation, mandatory BIS hallmarking, GST compliance and digital manufacturing technologies driving structural transformation of the sector
- Resilient Indian macro backdrop — FY25 real GDP growth of 6.5% with FY26 forecasts between 6.9% and 7%, driven largely by domestic consumption
- Government's recent decision to raise the effective import duty on gold expected to weigh further on demand; ratings agencies have flagged that organised gold jewellery sales volumes could see one of their weakest years in a decade
- US tariffs on Indian goods, which had reached as high as 50% in 2025, were reduced to an effective 18% following a bilateral trade deal announced in February 2026; for a domestic-facing jeweller the effect is indirect, via gold price volatility, import costs and consumer sentiment
- Trade agreements — the India-UK CETA alongside the existing India-UAE CEPA — expected to provide duty advantages and unlock long-term export opportunities for Indian jewellery manufacturers
- Rupee depreciation from roughly Rs 35 to Rs 87-88 against the US dollar over three decades acts as a persistent tailwind under Indian gold prices
- Success of the Ahmedabad flagship store reinforcing management's belief in the opportunity to build an organised retail jewellery network across Gujarat
- Antique bridal jewellery continues to enjoy strong customer acceptance owing to craftsmanship, design differentiation and emotional appeal during wedding purchases

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- End-to-end manufacturing strength — one of India's most established organised jewellery manufacturing set-ups, blending artisanal handcraft with precision machine-based production
- Diversified client base via a dual-channel model — institutional B2B clients across regional and national retail networks alongside its own B2C brand, Harit Zaveri
- In-house design and quality assurance capability, particularly in the lightweight and antique jewellery categories
- Established leadership in the Jadau, Meena and Kundan antique gold niche built over three decades
- Pan India wholesale distribution network reaching national, regional and local jewellers
- Legacy and deep-rooted promoter involvement supporting trust with institutional partners and retail customers
- Post-listing momentum since listing in FY24 — strengthened governance, reporting discipline and market visibility

non-obvious takeaways: Job work revenue decline was due to gold price inflation reducing kg volume, not demand loss — value of merchandise in B2B rose to INR843cr; inventory gain estimated at INR10-12cr, implying normalized PAT of INR9-10cr; retail margins are 3-4% higher than wholesale despite higher opex; 50-55% capacity utilization is sustainable due to gold price inflation doubling revenue without adding artisans
